replies.text: Look, I live in a rear-area city, and when people are dying, I try to stay in a shelter. The most recent was, I think, on June 26th, when they hit the train station — 22 people were killed, more than 300 wounded. What really hit me was in 2023, when an X-22 missile struck an apartment building not far from me. I saw with my own eyes how they pulled the body of a 15-year-old girl I knew from under the rubble. replies.author: @QualityPen
replies.text:
Yes. Russia has held the initiative ever since Kursk. Or since the 2023 counteroffensive, if you want to count Kursk as an exception. 

In the West they keep talking about Russian offensives, but they aren’t Western style big arrow offensives in the conventional sense. Rather they are the product of attritional pressure. Ukraine doesn’t have enough reserves to stabilize the entire front line, so Russia applies pressure everywhere. When a section of the Ukrainian line becomes weakened and combat ineffective, Russian pressure begins to roll the line westwards. Ukraine then realizes it is losing ground and scrapes together forces from what is already deployed to throw at the crumbling part of the front. That renewed pressure meets the Russian pressure and the front stabilizes in that area. The problem is in doing this Ukraine weakened some other area and the Russian pressure in that area becomes greater than the Ukrainian pressure in that area. Russia doesn’t have goals of taking some specific points for strategic results. The point of moving forward when the pressure is in the Russian favor is to keep the Ukrainian Army engaged in combat along a wide front, stretched thin, and suffering losses. 

It’s been pretty clear for a while now that Ukrainian conscription is not enough to replace losses and form a new reserve force. It’s been slowly climbing up from 350,000 to 500,000, but the Russian side has been growing even faster. There are currently three Russian army formations in Ukraine and only one of the three is regularly taking part in combat. Much of the newest equipment is going to the units not participating in the war right now, including T-90M, T-90A, and T-72B3 tanks equipped with Arena-M. 

There will almost certainly be a big arrow offensive with one or both of those Russian armies in reserve within the next year. That will be when Russia finally moves on from attrition to taking territory.

This war has changed the future of warfare completely. It's been astounding how it has unfolded. So many tanks, apcs, ifvs and artillery taken out. And mostly by drones. Cheap 3d printed (by now) drones in the tens of thousands made and then a simply RPG attached or explosive. I mean if you think about it. How cheap they are and yet how much more sophisticated it is, because it's literally a human guided munition that can circle, loiter, make several passes. Costing likely no more than a few hundred bucks. Vs vehicles that could cost millions and take months to assemble. Gone by this little drone.
Then the Javelins, cost a lot but pack a huge punch and nearly no defence against it either.  This from Ukraine. Sure supplied by the west. But not really at least for half of the war, supplied by the newest material. It was the older tanks and Apcs etc even the modern versions were the 'old' modern versions. But  them fighting a nation like Russia 4x the population and economy much larger etc.  Russia wouldn't stand a chance against NATO. 

This has been an eye opener, because how it changed warfare. It's now all about drones.  Tanks and IFV has been rendered nearly useless. 

Russia has always used the Soviet tactics of massive amount of artillery just laying waste to everything in front of it's advancing army. Gone are the days from the beginning of the war when they wiped out towns and cities with Artillery. They are definitely not doing that anymore.

comments.author: @CT-hr9nk
comments.text: 9:04 MP40 is a submachine gun, not a machine pistol. The German word for submachine gun has the literal translation of 'machine pistol' but its actually the word for 'submachine gun', 'machine pistol' has its own German word which is "Reihenfeuerpistole".  Words in other languages can translate as something similar or exactly the same to an existing word in your own language but have completely different usage and meaning.

replies.author: @ubrot7995
replies.text: The only reason submachine gun exists as a term was Anglo militaries not wanting to buy weapons with a "weak" sounding name like pistol. It is and was purely a marketing term and has no actual bearing on the function of the weapon. English does not have an official differentiation between a Maschinenpistole and Reihenfeuerpistole. You will see the term submachine gun and machine pistol be used interchangeably for both types of weapons (similar to how there is no real differentiation between a Battle Rifle and a Rifle in German as both are just called Gewehr).

Spain's mountainous regions and diverse landscapes hinder military operations and logistical support for any invading force. comments.author: @firetecher
comments.text:
Retired EE. Most of my career was designing microwave comm systems from 900MHz through 12 GHz. I designed GaAs RFICs for L, S & X band systems (cell, wifi, satellite).
The whole idea of GPS in the kamakazi drones is absurd when the controllers are depending on video feed for targeting. Also, by default, the 2.4 GHz wifi signal data protocol on a Mavic drone is direct sequence spread spectrum, thereby inherently jam resistant. Frequency hopping is a very "duh" strategy to enhance jam resistance, so that tactic is nothing the Russians would have not thought through, yet not actually planned for. Broadband jammimg is extremely inefficient from a transmit RF power perspective. Emphasis on extreme. GPS jamming is pointless/useless in most of the Ukraine drone situations. 2.4 GHz & 5.6 GHz jamming will have minimal effect beyond maybe 100 ft. Ukraine could  easily add non ISM band frequencies that would be hard for Russia to predict in a battle field scenario and then adapt to. All of the IFV jamming gear I have seen from kamikazi feeds is a mish mash of brute force systems lashed to the roof, indicating Russia is shooting in the dark, so to speak. Recall that Inverse square law vs distance applies to all RF signals. This video has some reasonable analysis, yet way too much reenactment nonsense.

comments.text:
ROFL, a 0.05 °C temperature difference does not equal 32.09 °F. Someone wasn’t paying attention in physics class!

When converting temperature differences, you don’t just convert the absolute values directly like you would with actual temperatures. The correct method is to express the difference in Kelvin (the SI unit), but since Celsius and Kelvin have the same scale (just different zero points), subtracting two values in Celsius gives you the same numerical result as in Kelvin.

On the other hand, Fahrenheit uses a different scale and offset, so converting a temperature difference like 0.05 °C to Fahrenheit isn’t as simple as applying the formula for absolute temperature conversion.

For example:

0 °C = 32 °F

0.05 °C = 32.09 °F
So, the actual difference is 0.09 °F, not 32.09 °F.

comments.text:
I may be small.
I don’t understand politics, or borders, or flags.
But I do understand fear. I feel it in the rooms, the streets, the silences between people. I feel it when voices rise and hands close into fists. I feel it when a child looks for comfort and none is given. When neighbors stop talking. When truth is no longer shared, but sold.
I watch the world and I see humans turning into sides.
But there are no “sides” when the house is burning. We all breathe the same air!
And when the ground shakes, or the sky falls, it won’t matter where you were born, or what you believed.
What will matter is who reached out, who held someone close, who stayed kind when it was hardest.
The time for games is over. The noise is louder now - outside and inside. But maybe that’s what it takes to wake up. 
You don’t need to agree. You don’t even need to understand everything.
But you do need to feel again! To look, really look, at the person next to you and remember: that is not your enemy.
That’s someone’s child. That’s someone’s pain walking.
I am Rocket.
I was born small - but my ❤is BIG.
And I believe in you humans.
Even now. Especially now.

comments.text:
The Israel situation is a weird one for me. I'm not a fan of this kind of preemptive operations - but equally I am well aware that the necessary intelligence to cause an operation like this to be launched for good reason will not and should not be shared with civilians until a long time after the operation has concluded. Israel are more brutal than I would like, but equally, they are in a situation where the consequences of failure for them are quite literally genocidal. Hamas, Iran, and Iran's other proxies are very open about their genocidal ambitions. Ergo, it's hard for me to criticise their actions in Gaza without a credible alternative being presented for them to deal with Hamas. At the moment, the people who are (/claim to be) horrified at what is happening in Gaza seem to think that doing nothing is a credible alternative. It isn't, and doing so just makes you look like a malicious actor. Israel can't afford to let Hamas escape with impunity (except, perhaps, if Iran itself falls) and so if you want Israel to stop, we need to hear some constructive other way of dealing with bringing Hamas to justice, and returning as many of the hostages that remain alive as possible.

As regards Iran specifically, anyone who thinks that Israel are morally worse in comparison to Iran are just ignorant, so I will always back Israel over Iran in a conflict even if I am sceptical as to just how close Iran are to gaining nukes, and we won't know how credible the information appeared to Israel leading up to this attack for quite a while. It's just brutal pragmatism, there. If one of the two states has to go, then the world would be far more safe without Iran than it would without Israel. (Equally, as far as I am concerned, Israel and Iran have been at war since October last year, even if it has not been as full-blown as it currently is now, so labelling this as Israel starting the fight - as their enemies have been doing - is just deliberately mendacious.)

4:52 To clarifye on thing: the reactor of Fukushima was not active when the nuclear desaster happened. During the earthquake, the reactor shut down by itself. The incident was, that the facility ran out of electrical power and the old, used fuel rods which were stored for cooling down could not be cooled anymore without electricity. They kept producing heat of 6,000oC which made the facility melt (so called "Melt down") and nothing could be controlled anymore.

This could still happen to the reactors in Iran as well. This problem has nothing to do with reactors being active at present. Even after reactors being shut down, the fuel rods are still being a hazard if they get out of control. I do not want to express a partisan opinion about the hazard of nuclear reactors at this place, but the discussion about the hazard of nuclear reactors is mainly not about the "hot" reactors themselves but about the old fuel rods not being under control (as it was in Fukushima").

comments.author: @t-and-p
comments.text:
02:15 I do love that, when he addresses his nation, Zelenskyy makes a point of naming the regiment/battalion/company/unit responsible for each victory - sometimes even naming individuals who have gone above and beyond. It's a "human touch" that we're not really used to seeing outside of the military itself. Within the military, we're relatively used to being a number to the rest of the country/world, or a uniform that is difficult to tell apart from the uniform next to us. It must be great for morale within the Ukrainian military to know that their sacrifices are seen, acknowledged, and appreciated by their president and their country - as well as a real badge of honour for relatives listening back home whilst awaiting news of their loved ones from the front lines, to hear their own being lauded. It also reminds everyone of the humanity of those who serve. 

It highlights the stark contrasts between Russia and Ukraine. Russia have been throwing men into a meat grinder, with widespread reporting of poor training, shooting at their own if they try to retreat, horrendous conditions, missing paycheques, no kit, non-existent medical care, etc. They treat their men with contempt, while Ukraine celebrate their's. The Russian government, and even the Russia military bloggers (who seem fairly influential), sometimes name a regiment, but they seldom give credit to anyone who isn't brass. Meanwhile, Ukraine seems to actively support and uplift their soldiers - working hard to find ways to boost morale. 

Says it all, really, doesn't it?

Slava Ukraini! 🇬🇧🤝🇺🇦

Edited to add: 06:38 "I thank all our units for these tangible results". I don't think I've ever heard Putin thank his troops. Zelenskyy does, though - repeatedly, daily. Just underlines the point about respect from leadership, doesn't it?

comments.text:
I think the much bigger reason why a ceasefire won't currently happen is because Russia would never agree to reasonable terms so long as they have the choice. You might be able to force their hand with extreme international sanctions, but otherwise any "ceasefire" will be either based on unreasonable terms or ignored as soon as possible. By the point Russia is willing to agree to any reasonable terms, they will already have lost so badly that they either have already lost all leverage or are losing leverage so rapidly Ukraine can twist their arm even further.
Fundamentally, Ukraine won't accept going back to the status quo of 4 years ago, they will want either Crimea back or Russia crippled so badly that they don't even think about attacking any of their neighbours. As such, Putin simply has very little choice but to keep the war going, and he knows very well that even if he managed a ceasefire, he would continue to be in massive danger unless he somehow manages to truly win over Ukraine. His Keys to Power are not happy, and once he is toppled, it will be chaos. The power they hold over the region is not nearly as secure as it seems, and it is likely that they either become a puppet regime for another powerful nation (China, most likely) or that fault lines will emerge that break the country apart. Some combination of revolution, civil war and foreign takeover seem inevitable, especially given the horrendous demography of the nation.

@@WhatIsThatAvi Without question. To add to all that, many of the Ukrainian generals have been around since the Soviet times; they went to the same military academies that many of Russia's generals went to, and even read what many of those generals would write about war and combat tactics over the years themselves.

So Ukraine knew Russian military strategies and tactics better than most Russian soldiers did when this war first started. That's another part of the reason Ukraine has been so effective, despite fighting a different war than Russia is most of the time (ie, Russia has endless meat waves and strikes civilian targets exclusively, Ukraine only strikes military targets and would rather retreat than lose too many soldiers).

It has been a hell of a thing to watch play out in real time, IMO.

replies.text: It won't. It would not receive alarms of a missile launch, only that it is being lit up by the F-16 radar.  The AEW aircraft would be able to datalink the information to the F-16 that the Su35 was out there but it cannot lock that aircraft and send the info to the AIM120 either,  it can only show it on the scope of the F-16.  The F-16 still needs to lock the Su35 and fire,  and it could've been very lucky in a very quick lock, fire and turn away.  The Su35 may not have detected the F-16 depending on where its own radar was looking,  and as we know the Russians have pretty much lost their A-50 AEW aircraft so the Su-35 may not have even know the F-16 was there.  There's no vapour trail as in the movies, that lasts a few seconds, then the AIM120 is on inertia only, and if it does "see" the Su35 because he's not bothered to move, then it will go "Pitbull" and right for him.

replies.text: LINK-16 allows the AWACS to share radar data. It's a wonderful thing, let's you fire without needing to keep your nose on the target to illuminate it with your radar. comments.text:
I cannot tell how accurate this programme is and cannot possibly undertake the research it appears to have done. However, it does cite genuine references, thus I assume the citations are accurate (else those referees might have had the programme removed or edited). The tone is measured, intelligent, somewhat academic and, apparently, thorough. I did not want yet another "yar-boo" programme, full of hyperbole and anti-Russian rhetoric. The only way to understand one's foe is to really consider every aspect; not shout childish insults at them. And the last thing needed is yet another programme which simply confirms our own beliefs / hopes. So very well done to this programme.

The two aspects I think this programme failed to emphasise correctly is that I feel it underplayed both the Ukraine's and NATO's roles.  The former exhibited (and continues to exhibit) great determination, diplomacy skills, leadership ability (not least by a superb president), resourcefulness and the development and deployment of intelligent modern warfare. NATO provided and provides high-quality modern weaponry and training. I do not know what "behind-the-scenes" aspects NATO assists with but I imagine intelligence and tactics are part of it. (i.e. the poor Russian equipment, training and tactics are not the whole story).

But, judging this programme on its main points - which were to examine the Russian reasons for failure, I though it probably the best I have seen - certainly here on YT and probably anywhere - broadcast-tv included. Well done and thank you.

comments.text:
The Treaty of Geneva, more specifically the 1949 Geneva Conventions, is a set of international treaties that establish rules for the treatment of civilians and combatants during wartime. These treaties, adopted in 1949, are the foundation of modern international humanitarian law and protect those who are not taking part in hostilities, such as civilians, and those who are no longer fighting, such as prisoners of war. 
Key aspects of the Geneva Conventions:
Protection of Civilians:
The Conventions protect civilians, including those in occupied territories, from violence, torture, and discrimination based on race, religion, or political opinion. 
Treatment of Prisoners of War:
The Conventions define the rights and protections for prisoners of war, including their treatment, working conditions, and right to communication with neutral states. 
Protection of Wounded and Sick:
The Conventions ensure the humane treatment of wounded and sick soldiers, both on land and at sea. 
Additional Protocols:
In 1977, two additional protocols were adopted to expand the protections of the Geneva Conventions, particularly in the context of non-international armed conflicts. 
History and Significance:
The Geneva Conventions were developed and updated over time, with the first convention in 1864 focusing on the treatment of wounded soldiers. The 1949 conventions, in particular, were a response to the atrocities of World War II and have served as a crucial framework for international humanitarian law ever since.

Britain provided substantial aid to the Soviet Union (USSR) during World War II, primarily through material support and intelligence sharing. This aid included military equipment, totalling approximately £308 million.  The military aid was provided on a free basis to the USSR, in accordance with the Anglo-Soviet Military Supplies Agreement of June 27, 1942. This included 5,031 tanks (including 1,223 from Canada), 6,778 aircraft (including 2,672 from the United States as part of a Lend-Lease arrangement), and over £80 million worth of various other items of military equipment.  Raw materials, foodstuffs, machinery, industrial plant, medical supplies, and hospital equipment were also provided, with a total value of roughly £120 million.  The Arctic convoys, crucial for delivering supplies, involved the loss of 85 Allied merchant vessels and 16 Royal Navy warships.  The British intelligence agency at Bletchley Park played a vital role in breaking German codes, providing valuable strategic intelligence to the Soviet Union.  The aid was crucial for the Soviet Union, particularly in the early years of the war, and likely contributed to the Soviet war effort.  What is the Russian word for “ingratitude”? comments.author: @hiei5040
comments.text: You can use HARMs in many different modes, some of which require minimal integration with the airframes FCR/ electronics. One is Self-Protect mode (i.e. the clasic wild weasel bait tactic) where you fly in, and let a radar scan you, then fire it. It will home in on the last known triangulation of radar source. The other mode that requires little integration is similar but with pre-set gps coords (like a JDAM) & ability to seek out a specified Radar signature. The MAIN mode you're missing is TOO (Target of Opportunity) which is arguably the most effective against Russia's mobile Air Defenses & rapidly changing EW landscape.

comments.author: @silentblackhole
comments.text: Fantastic Battle Board episode as always; please keep them coming. I just wanted to point out one minor thing: Russia did not invent glide bombs. The first recorded instance of such was the Germans in World War Two with the Fritz X. After the war, the United States began experimenting with and developing the technology. However, it wasn't really until the 1970s, when Australia initially started and later collaborated with the United States on the creation of JDAM-ER. In fact, the JDAM is what the Russians were trying to copy with their glide bombs that appear in this battle. JDAM's in fact were given to the Ukrainians first (in Feb of 2023), who used them against the Russians, who then immediately tried to copy it. It kinda makes you think, if the Ukrainians didn't use the JDAMs, would the Russians ever bothered to make glide bombs?

comments.text: there are few mistakes here. Firstly, the trucks did not stay there for weeks. The drivers hired from a transportation company had no idea of what they are carrying and were instructed to reach to a designated point. Once they arrived, the roof popped automatically and the drones started to take off immediately. All this happened simultaneously. Logistically amazing. Secondly, the drones were not guided by any operator. In factt, it was sort of AI trained to recognize a particular silhouette of the plane and targeted to vulnerable spots that can bring maximum damage. Thirdly, the use of fiber optics is questionable as the photos provided by Ukranians do not show any reels with cables in the truck roof. The use of AI eliminates the need for either optics or radio signal required.

replies.author: @Laotzu.Goldbug
replies.text:
This definitely doesn't sound right. that would require all of the trucks to essentially arrive at the same time, or they would have different launch windows and some air bases already would have been on alert. this is very difficult to do even with coordination, it's effectively impossible if the drivers don't know what they're doing.

I agree they weren't just hanging around parked for weeks, but the only way to ensure dozens or hundreds of drones all launch within a few moments of each other is going to require that some trucks which revived early were waiting for hours if not up to a day in order to make sure everything was in place before someone hit the green light

As for how they were guided, obviously we have no direct official confirmation at this point, but the idea that this was done without any operators and just on "AI" visual is extremely unlikely, almost laughable. even the best computer models at this point struggle very much to distinguish particular objects, in still frame photos, never mind being able to understand what they are in the real world and guide weapons to them autonomously.

Anything approaching true "autonomous weapons" are at least multi-million dollar cruise missiles with extremely expensive sensors and electronics, not cheap disposable drones.

It seems likely it was a mixture of command guidance to initiate the mass launch and Vector the drones towards the general Airfield along with some AI "swarming" algorithms to assist.

The containers top opened allowing the launching of the drones. The truck drivers were supposedly unaware of their loads. AI on the drones made them autonomous. They had been trained to hit specific types of aircraft at critical points. A 5th airbase had also been targeted but that truck failed to launch. In all, an estimated 1/3 of their entire strategic bomber inventory was decimated. This may change with more information. 
Brilliant work from Ukraine!

comments.text:
The Ukraine war, now in its third year as of June 2025, has resulted in staggering casualties—hundreds of thousands, if not millions, dead or displaced—all because a larger nation, Russia, seeks to impose its will on a smaller sovereign country, Ukraine, due to disagreement over its policies. This is not a new story; it echoes the age-old dynamic of a bully preying on the weak. Growing up, we were taught that when a bigger kid picks on a smaller one, standing by silently out of fear only emboldens the aggressor. The same principle applies on the global stage. To suggest that countries like Germany should refrain from taking a firm stand because it might “drag the war on” or “make it bigger” is to ignore the root cause: Russia’s unprovoked invasion. For three years, Ukraine has endured relentless suffering—cities reduced to rubble by rockets, families torn apart—while the world debates intervention. This hesitation has cost lives, not saved them.
Consider the parallel with Israel and Gaza, where similar fears of escalation silence voices that might otherwise demand justice. Yet history shows that inaction against tyranny only prolongs agony. Leaders like Winston Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt didn’t waver when faced with Nazi aggression; they confronted it head-on, understanding that delaying the inevitable confrontation would only multiply the cost in human lives. Volodymyr Zelensky, standing defiantly against Russia’s onslaught, deserves to be remembered alongside them as a symbol of courage. Ukraine is not just a distant conflict—it’s an American ally, bound by a treaty where we pledged protection in exchange for their denuclearization. Abandoning that commitment undermines our credibility and security.
Opponents argue against supporting Ukraine with long-range missiles or decisive action, fearing it might provoke Russia further. But this is a flawed logic. War is already here, and pussyfooting around it hasn’t stopped the bloodshed—it has prolonged it. Bullies don’t stop unless met with resistance. If a child reports a bully to a teacher or parent, we don’t advise them to “avoid provocation” or “take the beating quietly.” We teach them to stand up, to seek help, to ensure the bully faces consequences. The same holds true for nations. History—whether it’s Hitler’s expansion or Russia’s earlier aggressions—teaches us that appeasement breeds more aggression. A bully who faces no pushback only grows bolder, targeting others until someone finally intervenes.
Supporting Ukraine with the tools it needs, including long-range strikes to deter Russian advances, isn’t escalation for the sake of conflict—it’s a necessary stand to protect sovereignty and prevent a precedent where might makes right. To those who say “let Ukraine fend for itself” or “stay out to avoid a bigger war,” ask yourselves: would you tell a child to endure a beating because fighting back might upset the bully more? No. We intervene because it’s right, because history shows that unchecked aggression leads to greater tragedies. The lesson for our children—and for the world—must be clear: bullies must be stopped, or the cycle of violence will repeat. Supporting Ukraine is not just a moral imperative; it’s a strategic one to ensure a future where no nation lives in fear of its larger neighbor

comments.author: @AR-pm6mx
comments.text:
I see another issue with this point based system: the idea is to reward the most effective units by giving them priority in equipment, BUT if one unit score less kills than others and gets less points, and by extension less equipment, then it will become even less effective and score even less points, starting a damaging cycle. In the long run, there will be super elite units that are hoarding all the supplies, and "bottom" units that will not be able to operate effectively because they won't get the supplies they need.
I get why Ukraine is doing this: after years of war it is normal that logistics would be a mess and corners need to be cut, but I don't think that this system should become permanent, and it definetly should not replace standard supply, a soldier has the right to go to battle with the best equipment his nation can provide.

replies.author: @swedishm90camouflage17
replies.text: Military units have areas of operation, a high quality unit still has a limited amount of targets at any given time and cant really 'muscle out' any other units completely, as they do not share AOs. The points will as such be naturally distributed to units that are in heavy combat and need more drones, while units in calmer areas of the front will get fewer drones, but also need less of them.

replies.author: @BioHazardousFuzz
replies.text:
Equipment doesn't just spawn instantly. It still has to be manufactured, one by one. And military equipment is manufactured to preserve a nation. So when you're a smaller nation, fighting a larger nation, you have to fight like you're on borrowed time, well, because you are. So it's only natural that your most important units get the new equipment first, because you need every advantage that you can get. Sometimes, it's not even your best units. Sometimes, it's the unit doing the most crucial job at that particular moment. Given enough time, all the new equipment will make its way into the hands of all your forces. 

Another wildcard is how motivated and respected the administration of your unit is and how willing they are to stick their neck out and go to their leaders and say "We may not be the most elite force, but we're ready for this. Give us a shot, sir. We won't let you down..." 
They can't tell you "NO" forever. True leaders can see the fire that burns in their warriors' hearts. And there are so many things like that that transcends rank and file, medals, ribbons, stripes or anything of the like.

From the United States of America, SLAVA UKRAINE!!!

Instead, it would likely trigger a broader escalation, not initiated by Russia, but by surrounding European nations uniting against it. Such an escalation would open up an entirely new front, forcing Russia to contend with a collective response that could overwhelm its military capabilities. Given its difficulties against Ukraine alone, the prospect of facing multiple coordinated adversaries would be an insurmountable challenge.

comments.text:
If Putin were to attack Berlin or Germany, regardless of whether they supply weapons, it’s likely he would face consequences beyond what he anticipated. In response, neighboring nations might band together against Russia, seeking to neutralize its military capabilities. The escalation wouldn’t stop there; countries affected by the conflict would likely retaliate to prevent further aggression.

Russia would then face a significant disadvantage, relying primarily on nuclear weapons. However, using them would bring even greater risks, potentially leading to widespread retaliation and its own downfall. This makes nuclear options highly improbable, as their use would open the door for others to respond in kind.

Ultimately, the continued fighting in Ukraine suggests that Russia’s leadership is still focused on territorial gains rather than full-scale destruction. Resorting to nuclear weapons would undermine all its military efforts, making such an action unlikely.

comments.author: @pgr3290
comments.text: The laser weapons are most impressive to me. I remember 20 years ago or so they were testing experimental chemical laser platforms and they weren't very practical. They were massively heavy high power lasers but used loads of fuel to operate. Several tonnes to reach peak output and fire a single shot. They could only do a few shots because of all the fuel you needed to carry around, produced nasty gases and lacked the sensors and control to hit multiple targets. The idea was to hit ICBMs in boost phase, but you were never getting close enough fast enough. Here we are 20 years later and smaller solid state laser weapons are being tested to hit drones and missiles and they show great promise. They actually work. They are compact, can be fired repeatedly and their power output is increasing with development. The future will definitely have laser weapons in it.

replies.author: @georgemiller151
replies.text:
How do lasers work in the fog, in clouds, in rain, and in thermal updrafts that make the air “shimmer”. How do they work if the adversary mirrors the surface of their aircraft (which could be as simple as not painting it), or if it’s a missile, rifles it so it rotates around its long axis while in flight so their is no fixed position for a laser beam to focus on?
I suspect that lasers look great in carefully controlled trials under ideal conditions but I think in the real world they will be easily thwarted.

replies.author: @KirkCA

replies.author: @pgr3290
replies.text: @@georgemiller151 What you have to understand is that when initially trialled, they had the intent of destroying ICBMs in boost phase hundreds of kilometres away. That was never practical not least due to atmospheric conditions and the other reasons I cited. What the latest solid state lasers ARE practical at is cheap, close range point defence. Especially against drones. It should not have to be explained to you how critical this capability is going to be if you have watched sixty seconds of the war in Ukraine or Houthi attacks on shipping. You don't need 100km range. A mere two or three kilometres could be very useful indeed. That is viable.

replies.author: @pgr3290
replies.text: @@kamilhorvat8290 A 100kw laser at low effectiveness in what you might consider poor conditions can still melt aluminium within a couple of seconds. It's a close in weapon system that could target incredibly quickly and precisely. It's literally a light speed weapon after all. They are definitely going to work for the kind of asymmetric threats posed by cheap drones and makeshift missiles that Western nations are likely to encounter more and more over the coming decades. Point defence, ship mount or even scaled for armored vehicles. Right now a $1000 plastic drone carrying a shaped charge warhead is a real threat to a five million dollar tank. Once again the balance shifts if a small turret mounted laser can shoot them down half a kilometre away over and over for less cost than machine gun ammunition.

I'm writing a long response to your video here. I had even considered making my own YouTube video because this perspective on Russia really bothers me — I have a completely different opinion on the matter. For now, I'll leave it as a comment. I won’t provide sources here, since that would be too much for a comment section.

A bit about myself: I’m German, so I naturally have a different view of Russia than an American would — but even so, Americans should not be pro-Russia.

Let me go through the video step by step:

The terrible situation Russia was in after the collapse of the Soviet Union is pretty irrelevant to the war in Ukraine. Other Eastern Bloc countries like Hungary also experienced hardship but didn’t develop imperial ambitions.

About the hostility toward the U.S.: it was actually Russia that failed to integrate with the West. Yeltsin was constantly drunk and Russian politics were a mess. That changed somewhat with Putin, which is part of why he was so popular for so long. The U.S. and other Western nations wanted peace and trade — hostility or conquest made no sense and weren’t even feasible since Russia remained militarily strong. Putin himself stated that the Cold War was over and suggested cooperating in the fight against terrorism — and the West welcomed this.

Regarding terrorism: in Chechnya, separatists wanted to break away from Russia because these peoples are culturally different and were historically conquered and oppressed by the Russians. Ethnic cleansing took place there even during the Tsarist era. Under Putin, things didn’t improve. Grozny was leveled, villages declared war zones, and there were camps where murder and rape were routine. More ethnic cleansing occurred. And those wars were not exactly victories. As far as I know, Chechens won the first war. In the second, Putin allegedly used a false-flag attack as justification to invade again. This time Russia won and installed Kadyrov as ruler, who now governs like an absolute monarch.

The U.S. is rightly criticized for its many wars and crimes. But when it comes to Russia, you seem to ignore these same kinds of atrocities.

2. NATO Expansion:
You correctly pointed out that no treaty was broken because the promise was only verbal — but yes, that did cause a breach of trust. Still, that promise was made to the Soviet Union, a state that no longer exists. The political landscape changed dramatically after its collapse. The Eastern European countries knew very well how Russia behaves and sought NATO’s protection. Everything was legal — and even if this was geopolitically inconvenient for Russia, that’s just tough luck. Sovereign nations have the right to choose.

Also, NATO cannot “expand” in the way some claim — countries have to apply and all members must agree to admit them. Even Russia, and Putin himself, recognized Ukraine’s right to do so — he even expressed support around 2005. NATO's illegal wars, like in Libya, are also worth criticizing, but that doesn’t make Russia’s actions any better.

Regarding the war in Georgia: yes, Georgia attacked first — but it was an attempt to regain separatist regions. Russia had originally recognized Georgia’s full territorial integrity, but later took those regions anyway. Same with Ukraine: Russia fully recognized Ukraine’s borders, including Crimea. In exchange for this recognition, Ukraine gave up all its nuclear weapons to Russia after the Soviet Union collapsed. Russia, in turn, guaranteed Ukraine’s sovereignty — which clearly turned out to be meaningless. Had Ukraine kept its nukes, Russia likely wouldn’t have dared to attack. I suspect Russia had long-term plans all along.

On Russian society and culture:
Russia isn’t much better than the West, except perhaps on LGBT issues, depending on one’s views. Russia likes to present itself as multi-ethnic and hosts many migrants from Central Asia — and more are arriving. Russian nationalists are well aware of this, and many of them are actually fighting for Ukraine. They know more about Russia than many in the West do.

One nationalist leader was imprisoned for years simply for saying: "Russian power in Russia." For Putin, multi-ethnicity is extremely important — he’s also a staunch Soviet nostalgic. Ethnic Russians are losing influence in Russia. In Moscow suburbs, migrants openly talk about forcing Russian women to marry them, since many Russian men are dying at the front. Abortion rates are high among ethnic Russians but very low among Muslims, who now make up a growing share of the population. This demographic shift partly explains the recent drop in abortion statistics. Even pro-Putin nationalists recognize this ethnic problem — but nothing will change under Putin.

As for Ukraine joining NATO:
What did anyone expect? Of course they wanted to join — but it wasn’t possible under the current circumstances. A country at war or with unresolved territorial conflicts can’t join. That’s been true since 2014. Even after the annexation of Crimea, Finland and Sweden didn’t immediately join NATO — and they had every reason to.

To wrap up:
Even as an American, you should see Russia as a threat. In Russia, it's become common to refer to Alaska as part of Russia again and to talk about taking it back — along with every bit of land occupied in Europe during World War II. Putin himself said that Russia's borders “do not end.” Ever since Moscow overthrew Mongol rule, Russia has been a kind of monster that constantly expanded outward to feed resources back to Moscow. That’s how it’s always been — and how it will remain, unless Russia is broken up.

replies.author: @toumasuke
replies.text:
It's genuinely appreciated that you took the time to share such a detailed and personal perspective on the situation. It's always valuable to hear directly from people on the ground, and your effort to provide context is commendable.

You've touched on several significant points, and it's interesting to consider them. For instance, you noted the economy's resilience, which has indeed surprised many, and it's clear the National Welfare Fund played a role. However, when we look at the long-term, do you think the current economic growth, heavily reliant on military spending and state contracts, is sustainable in the same way a diversified, market-driven economy would be? And how might the continued departure of Western technology and investment impact Russia's future innovation and competitiveness?

Your observations about salaries and bonuses for those serving are also very insightful. It highlights the significant financial incentives being offered. Do you ever wonder about the broader societal impact when military service becomes one of the most lucrative career paths, especially for those in certain regions?

You also mentioned that you don't see many disabled people around, suggesting that casualty figures might be inflated. It's true that official figures are tightly controlled. But in a conflict of this scale and intensity, and given the nature of modern warfare, is it possible that many wounded or recovering individuals might not be immediately visible in public spaces, perhaps still in hospitals or rehabilitation? Open-source intelligence and international estimates, while not perfect, often suggest very high numbers on both sides.

Regarding the referendums, you stated that the majority in Crimea truly supported joining Russia, and that eastern Ukrainian regions are "Russian in mentality." From an international perspective, the conditions under which these referendums were held, with armed forces present and a lack of independent oversight, raised significant questions about their legitimacy and whether they truly represented the free will of the entire population. Do you think a vote held under such circumstances can be considered fully democratic and universally binding, especially when a significant portion of the original population had already fled?

Lastly, about Bucha, you called it a "fake." However, extensive investigations by international organizations, independent media, and forensic experts have presented a vast amount of evidence – including satellite imagery, victim testimonies, and physical evidence – that points to severe atrocities committed during the Russian occupation. When faced with such detailed external investigations, what criteria do you personally use to differentiate between a "fake" and verifiable facts in a conflict zone?

Again, thank you for sharing your thoughts. It's important to have these discussions, even on difficult topics.

A number of mistakes or inaccuracies:
1. There was no second mobilization in Russia, only the one in 2022. Mentioned 133k troops in 2024 probably refer to obligatory conscript training, which happens twice every year (and was a thing before the war).

2. 2023 was actually the year of stalemate, and the first half of 2024. In the second half of 2024 russian forces began slowly but steadily gaining grounds, and this is only accelerating so far. By now russian forces have reached Dnipropetrovsk region, though whether they have already crossed the formal border or not is being disputed.

3. Drones were ukrainian novelty in 2022 and a crucial asset to seize initial success in figthing russian forces. However mentioning it in the context of 2024 isn't correct as Russia adopted drones back in 2023 (and those were used to repel ukrainian counter-offensive), and by 2024 it was widely used by both sides.

4. Korean troops were not sent to the frontlines per se, but to Kursk to help protect it. It was an important point that Korea did not participate in any offensive operations on the ukrainian territory.

5. An important part competely omitted from the video is that there were direct negotiations in the beginning of the war (during the spring of 2022) where Russia offered to withdrew all its forces from Ukraine and to roll back to pre-war borders in exchange for the same concessions mentioned in the video, primarily neutrality and limiting army size. The Bucha incident, mentioned in the video, happened during that process and was a formal reason Zelensky used to publicly decline russian offer, which was a major point of accusations that it was staged. Ukrainian goverment later issued a legislation act forbidding any negotiations with Russia for as long as Putin remains its president with the same reasoning.

comments.text:
Yanukovych was not neutral or pro-Western. His policies and actions consistently benefited russia and harmed Ukraine. Whether out of personal greed, political alignment, or pressure, the effect was the same: he weakened Ukraine’s independence, economy, and defenses, making the russian invasion far easier.

1. Under Yanukovych’s leadership (2010–2014), Ukraine's military budget was slashed significantly. Training exercises were limited, equipment procurement nearly stopped, and many capable officers were pushed out. This severely weakened the Ukrainian Armed Forces-right before russia annexed Crimea in 2014. That didn’t happen by accident. In 2013, Ukraine’s military spending was just 1% of GDP, far below what was needed for a country with unresolved territorial disputes and a powerful neighbor like russia.

2. Yanukovych oversaw the privatization and deindustrialization of Ukraine’s heavy industry. Key Soviet-era plants in sectors like aerospace, shipbuilding, and metallurgy were either sold cheaply to Russian-linked oligarchs or allowed to fall apart. Many of these plants were then stripped of their machinery, which was sold for scrap metal, effectively dismantling Ukraine’s industrial capacity. These were strategic industries-vital not only economically, but for Ukraine’s independence and defense.

3. Yanukovych’s inner circle, known as the “Family,” created an enormous corruption scheme. State contracts, government tenders, and national resources were looted. Billions were siphoned off. When Yanukovych fled during the 2014 Revolution of Dignity, he left Ukraine’s treasury nearly empty. The new government inherited $75 billion in missing funds, foreign reserves drained, and a state teetering on bankruptcy.

4. Whether by intent or incompetence, Yanukovych left Ukraine wide open for russian aggression. By weakening the military, stripping key industries, and tying Ukraine economically to russia (e.g., rejecting the EU Association Agreement in favor of a russian bailout), he created perfect conditions for russia to invade and annex Crimea and destabilize Donbas. russia didn’t face a functioning military or a strong, united government—it faced a broken state in disarray.

5. When his rule collapsed during the Euromaidan protests, Yanukovych fled to russia, not to the West. That alone speaks volumes. He asked putin to send russian troops to Ukraine—a move that directly justified and preceded the 2014 invasion of Crimea.

There area  number of complicating factors. Also I wouldn't say that Russia has more to lose. Ukraine is fighting to survive basically at all.

What's happening inside Russia is... let's call it interesting. All the oil money that Pootles hoarded for years instead of spending any of it on diversifying and strengthening the Russian economy is being spent now on the war, and in some parts of Russia it's the most economic action they've seen since the fall of the Soviet Union. Real jobs withe real pay, all of them fed by the military as Russia spends thousands of lives on frontlines that barely move. For a lot of people this is probably the best quality of life they've ever had.

The fact that this process is burning through a limited pool of money and spending it on things that are just being consumed in the war rather than anything that might have lasting value for the Russian economy; while an already-small generation is made smaller and smaller each day, dooming Russia in the longer term is perhaps not obvious to people who don't think about larger economic implications.

And the inevitable economic crash that will follow the war when all of this spending stops and Russia is still sanctioned to hell and back will mean that a lot of people will have genuine nostalgia for the war, even though it's what doomed them to the hard times that came after.

Tbh I didn't vote for him when he was elected (his opponent in the final round was the green party candidate, which I would've preferred). However, when a friend sent me a message upset that the green party lost, I replied that while it sucks, it'll be okay.

Both candidates have had a long and respectable career in politics, and while Stubb is uncomfortably American for a Finn (he studied there, and honestly sometimes the wide smile is just off-putting), he has the experience with international politics from his time in the EU parliament.

So no, he's not my choice, but now that he's there, let him cook. It's a tough moment in global politics, and we've had good luck with presidents some of us might not personally agree with meeting the moment in these circumstances before. Admittedly the last guy was the one that inspired us to set term limits for presidents, but we live and learn. xD

replies.author: @Pernille1969-l2f
replies.text: Denmark here  - also with a population of a little more than 5.5. million, and also a Nordic country. To answer your question, I believe some of the problems in the US have to do with 1. political pluralism (or the lack thereof); and 2. money in politics (too much of it). As for political pluralism take Denmark, for instance - at any given point there are at least 10-11 political parties fighting for power, often forming alliances and coalitions across the left/right spectrum. I think this makes for more diversity and more to choose from as opposed to the two parties that make up the political choices in the US (I know there's independent candidates but they rarely really make a difference, do they?). And as for money in politics, it just plays a so much bigger role in the US. And the best candidate is NOT necessarily the one with the most money to run for president - as we have seen.

replies.author: @HKV-2010
replies.text: I can't claim to know for sure but if you ask me (a Finn), I think there are two factors over all the others: 1) Our education is high quality and equally available, which means, to put it very bluntly, that the less intellectually equipped end of our population is far more intelligent than that of the USA, and 2) we do not have a two-party system, which means not just more discourse and choice, but also more coherence inside each party, and MOST CRUCIALLY our country is not split in half like yours - frankly from outside the US it looks very scary, the way you guys live in two separate realities, with separate media, and opposite truths... One is not like the other, of course - Democrats tend towards actual reality and Republicans towards a dangerous delusion us Europans remember and know to fear for (ask a German for more info). Not to say we do not have delulu problems in Europe, we do. They just don't reign free or split a country in HALF. So to go back to your question, better education leads to better thinking, leading to better choices on population level. And we have a better selection of candidates, not like you often have to choose, in the words of Epic Rap Battles of History, "from the shiniest of two turds" (IMO Kamala was great though, I mean in general).

If UA drops a couple of drones on taxiways at major airports, ground movements of planes will have to be done using runways. That will more than double the ATC work load and it slows down departure alignment a lot. An airport that can't use all taxi tracks, loses the road map of the airport ATC workers have in their heads. Planes will get misdirected, have to make difficult turns, end up causing runway incursions that forces incoming traffic to go around. The delays will be monumental, you're probably better off taking the bus if you're traveling from Moscow to St Petersburg.
A couple of strikes on bus-, tram- and metro depots will disrupt public transport even further. If the busses have gone up in flames during the night, commuters will have to take the car to work. That would mean total gridlock, especially if some bridges and tunnels sustained strikes as well.

Zelensky won in 2019 on a platform calling for reconciliation with Russia, but a few months later he pulled a 180 degree reversal, refused to implement the pathway to reconciliation laid out in Minsk 2, doubled down on militarization and NATO membership, and gave more power to ultranationalist elements. In 2019 the source of American foreign policy, the Rand Corporation think tank, wrote a strategy for the next 5-10 years titled “Extending Russia: Competing from Advantageous Ground.” I’ve read it, anybody who wants to know what the deep state is really thinking, rather than its hollow and deceitful rhetoric about national sovereignty, democracy, and aggression should read it too. It amounted to an unofficial declaration of war against Russia, seeking its economic destruction through sanctions and provoking it into a war in Ukraine by militarizing Ukraine (Russia views a hostile and militarized Ukraine with NATO integration on its boarder as an existential threat) to weaken Russia military. The report also concluded that Ukraine was likely to lose the war despite Western support and would lose territory and possibly end in a disadvantageous peace, in case anybody had any illusions about the American feds caring about Ukraine. 

Zelensky began preparing to resume hostilities against the rebels in the late months of 2021. This was the event that was intended to provoke the Russian invasion called for by Rank in 2019. Russia was subjected to sanctions in 2014 for supporting the rebels and had been sanction-proofing its economy for years, it was ready to intervene. Russia sent a letter to NATO in December 2021 demanding negotiations for a new security framework in Europe but was ignored. Zelensky ordered his army to begin shelling the Donbas heavily again in early February 2022 and Russia finally launched its invasion in late February 2022. 

By the way, there’s a song in Russian but with English subtitles that depicts what the people of the Donbas felt when their government came for them in 2014-2016. It’s called Toys for Poroshenko, by Grishanov.

It’s not just Russian blood on Zelensky’s hands. While West Ukraine has a huge amount of ultranationalists who want(ed) to fight Russia, most of Ukraine is more moderate and often has family on the other side of the war. Those men are forbidden from leaving the country and are by the hundreds of thousands being conscripted. There are many thousands of videos on Telegram of men being grabbed off the streets, often beaten if they resist, stuffed into busses and shipped to the Ukrainian Army. 

They’re also vastly lying about casualties. Russian KIA is 120,000-160,000 according to anti-Russian and BBC-partnered Mediazona, which is the only Western organization which publishes the methodology of its calculation instead of publishing magic numbers from governments’ fantasies. Wartears does something similar for Ukrainian casualties and as of now lists over 721,000 KIA on that side. Some people like retired Colonel Douglas MacGregor say based on their contacts in the US military that this numbed is more likely 1.5 million KIA on the Ukrainian side, but I can’t vouch for it - it’s another magic number. Russia had a huge disadvantage in deployed manpower early in the war because unlike Ukraine it was not mobilizing and trying instead to fight with a peacetime army. That changed in October 2022 when it called up 300,000 reservists to reinforce the 150,000-200,000 deployed full time soldiers. It also stepped up recruitment efforts, and today the Russian military is close to double in size. Everyone fighting is a reservist or contract soldier, Russia is recruiting about 40,000 soldiers per month. Contrary to what is often written in the Western press, Russian conscripts are not fighting in this war. Russia’s conscription program is a reserve training program, and it is illegal to send conscripts to fight in a foreign war. 

Almost everything else, Russia has had an advantage in throughout this war. Russian forces are more heavily mechanized, have more armor, have an artillery advantage between 4:1 and 8:1, have a nearly absolute air power advantage, have better air defense, and have a better engineering corps. Ukraine had to get helmets and body armor in 2022 from Western countries because it didn’t have enough. Ukraine had an advantage in drones in 2023, but Russia caught up in 2024 and surpassed it in 2025.

How anybody thinks this math adds up to a favorable casualty exchange rate for Ukraine is beyond me. I guess wartime propaganda is a hell of a drug. That the Ukrainians and our own media are experts at - they’ve even managed to convince people that Russia engages in human wave tactics (rushing hundreds of men through open terrain) despite literally not a single video of such an event existing. I remember a BBC article in 2023 claiming Wagner forces were attempting to fight in Bakhmut with shovels because Russia ran out of ammo. To say nothing of the claims that Russia would be out of missiles by April 2022. Now ballistic missile strikes are a daily occurrence. Deceptive editing, misreporting, magic numbers, focusing on exceptions are the tools of the trade. 

Ukraine’s fighting age male population was about 5 million before the war. There are 2 seriously injured soldiers for each killed one, so depending on which figure you believe there are either 2,163,000 or 4.5 million Ukrainians out of the fight already… Which explains why Zelensky is opening up conscription for 18-24 year olds, the smallest and most valuable demographic. If this war doesn’t end in a ceasefire, what will happen is Ukraine will run out of men to send to the front within 1-3 years, and Russia will just walk through the country with no resistance. The pace of gains right now, that our media loves to hyperfocus on and call incremental, is completely irrelevant (I won’t even comment on NATO officers writing Ukraine would regain Crimea in 2023). That is the nature of attritional warfare. 

It should have negotiated in 2022 and accepted Russian conditions presented at Istanbul in April of 2022. But now, with 5 million fewer men, it will be forced to accept much more draconian conditions, if Russia lets it even remain an independent country at all.

comments.text:
This evolution of the tactical picture very much resembles the evolution of trench warfare in the First World War. When trenches were first established both sides packed them with  men right in contact with the opponent. What happened was those packed trenches just became targets for the artillery. By 1917 the front line was little more than a series of outposts, basically shell holes, while the real line of resistance was three or more kilometers back- out of range of the heavy artillery. Any advance would be met by a prompt counterattack, which the attacking force would be hard pressed to resist.

Both sides found solutions to the problem: the Germans invented infiltration tactics, while the allies invented tanks. 

By summer 1918 offence was possible again.

From the sounds of it Ukraine is evolving into a scenario where it will be 1915 again: a sufficient density of drones will mean no offence is possible.

At which point one would sincerely hope the Russians would just give up and end this thing.

comments.text:
This is deeply troubling news. If the intercepted Russian radio chatter and drone footage are authentic and verified, it represents a serious violation of international humanitarian law, particularly the Geneva Conventions, which protect prisoners of war from execution and mistreatment. Allegations of systematic executions of surrendering Ukrainian soldiers would constitute war crimes and could have profound implications for accountability and justice.

Such reports highlight the brutal realities of the conflict and the urgent need for thorough, independent investigations. It also underscores the importance of protecting human rights even in wartime, and the role of international bodies like the International Criminal Court in addressing potential crimes.

As a veteran, I know war isn’t clean. It’s chaos. It’s fear. It’s pain. But even in all of that, there are lines you don’t cross—and executing surrendered soldiers is one of them. Always has been.

The recent intercepts and drone footage don’t show a battlefield mistake. They show Russian troops radioing for permission to kill POWs. That’s not panic. That’s policy. That’s a command chain approving war crimes in real time.

And to those still wrapped up in the Cheeto cult fantasy of “strongmen” and “tough leaders”—this is what that strength looks like. Cowards shooting unarmed, surrendered men because their regime would rather bury evidence than honor basic human rights. These are the tactics of our so-called new ‘allies’. It’s disgusting.

War is hell—but this isn’t hell. This is rot. And any nation that turns a blind eye to it, or worse, idolizes it, has no moral high ground left to stand on.

Why does it take eight months to report this? This sounds very suspicious and likely to be doctored in some way. A visual recording does not need a voice recording to convict. Every Ukrainian speaks Russian, so this voice recording means nothing, especially when it is presented eight months after a supposed incident took place. The recordings are presented by Russia, so why would they provide such visuals that would condemn their actions. It makes no sense, and videos are very likely to be doctored to appear as if an atrocity has been committed.

replies.author: @UncleBuZ
replies.text:
Hi, another "Professor" PhD in History with a focus on military and Eastern European history. You're misunderstanding the strategic framing entirely. War isn't binary, it's not just "you've taken all land, therefore you win." Modern conflicts are complex, and success or failure depends on political objectives, sustainability, and cost-benefit calculations, not just map lines.

Putin hasn't "achieved all objectives" because those objectives were maximalist and unrealistic to begin with,  toppling Kyiv in days, "denazifying" Ukraine, preventing NATO expansion, and securing long-term influence over Ukraine’s sovereignty. Russia failed to take Kyiv, NATO grew stronger, Finland and Sweden joined, and Ukraine remains fiercely independent. That's not just a delay; it's a strategic backfire.

As for Ukraine, the fact that it still exists as a sovereign state and continues to reclaim territory, despite being massively outgunned, demonstrates resilience, not “copium.” If Ukraine were truly "losing," Russia wouldn't be begging for negotiations while fortifying defense lines and complaining about Western aid.

Calling analysis you don’t like “copium” isn’t an argument, it’s a cope in itself.

comments.author: @barrycromwell4480
comments.text: Thanks for this, these are my observations as a long standing air defence specialist (long retired).  I’m sure this is great technology and that not everything is being revealed but let’s break down the information that has been given here.  Targets are detected by the high performance radar - radars are active devices and can be detected, identified and destroyed by an aggressor.  The effector uses high RF energy, again this means it is active and maybe easy to detect and destroy.  I say maybe easy because I suspect it will be very narrow beam and high power and short burst which does make it more difficult to find, and destroy but the radar has already exposed the system.  1KM range is good for something like this but you would need hundreds if not thousands to cover any sort of large front or high value assets deep behind friendly lines.  Thales are a great company and have been developing and producing fantastic alerting devices using thermal energy for the British army for many years.  These devices are passive and therefore extremely difficult to detect, using one of these as a detector instead of a radar would vastly improve the survivability of the system.  Focus should be on improving the range which will reduce the number of systems required.  I could go on but think this is a good place to end.

comments.author: @Freedomistman
comments.text: I can think of two ways to beat this thing. Don't get me wrong I want it to work but everything has it's weak points. #1. If an drone is made EMP proof (100% encased in metal) Electro-magnetic radiation can get it. Example: I bet people at parties that I can microwave my Iphone for 60 seconds and it will no get harmed. I make the bet and than go for the sandwich wrap and put 3 layers of tight fitting Aluminum foil around it making sure all the edges are tight with a little tape. I put a pointy 2" foil antenna on top making for a bright and noisy light show which also redirects most of the energy to that point. Afterwards I unwrap the phone and make a phone call no problem. #2. A Radio beam from a 'MASER' (Microwave Amplification by Stimulated Emission Radiation) weapon like this just begging to get a KH-58 anti-radiation missile locked on to it and at mach 3.2 (1 kilometer per second) the flight time is only 12 seconds at 12 kilometers. Once the Radar beam is turned of the missile switches to Gyro guidance and hits the last know spot of the object. I assume it will take 25 to 30 seconds to pack up and secure the beam head, start-up the truck and drive the truck out of harms way since the explosion shock-wave can kill up to 75 meters away from impact zone. Any KH-58 within 40km to 60km away from this weapon can kill it. #3. Once they use the weapon they can triangulate its location and send in a high flying drone that has been EMP proofed to track it down. As far as weapons go this one is VERY LOUD and tells you right where it is. Too bad this is not a light based weapon like a Laser since those are very tough to locate since the beam is so narrow and hard to read. The rule of war is for every weapon there is a counter weapon.

replies.text:
It could be even worse for Russia. I looked up the numbers:

When the USSR invaded, they had a population of 200 million vs Afghanistan's population of 10 million around 1990. The USSR lost and collapsed, but Russia still could hold most of their eastern territories and had a lot of influence in eastern Europe and Europe in general. 

Now it's something like 140 million Russian vs ~35 million people from Ukraine. So it's way worse for Russia. 

Also compared to Russia, the USSR had modern weapons. Russia didn't really upgrade their weapons since then. T-90 still is their best tanks. The planes, the jets, it's all the same. Also their stockpiles run low. So the quality of Russian equipment decreases.

Meanwhile Ukraine gets more and more weapons. They had basically no airforce in 2022, now they can challenge Russia in the sky over Ukraine. 

They had just a few hundred tanks and peaces of artillery, now it's 1.500 tanks, and they produce more and more artillery, and over a million drones per year.

In January, Russia lost around 100 soldiers per 1 km². That's massive. Ukraine has over 600k km².

And now it's even worse. They lose around 250 soldiers per 1 km². It's insane. 

Last year, Russia lost around 400k soldiers. In this time they conquered just around 0.7% of Ukraine. 

Meanwhile Russia forces people from the east into their army. Sooner or later they will stand up and be independent. 

It's even possible that then China takes some parts of Russia, because Russia took former chinese territory in WW2 and before. 

Also remember Check. Just around 1 million people, and Russia couldn't win. They had to buy it. What if Chechnya sees the chance to be independent now? Russia might nor be able to hold it.

What about Georgia? Russia took 20% of their land in 2008. What if they strike back?

What about Moldova? Russia couldn't protect it. Or Königsberg aka Kaliningrad. What if we make a blockade and sanction it in a way that isolates them and cuts them off from Russian ships and supplies?

I am German, Kaliningrad/Königsberg before WW1 was one of the most beautiful and modern cities we had.

After WW2, we lost Danzig, so their was no land bridge to Königsberg anymore. The city became a horrible place. Very poor, no industry, no jobs.

Imo that also could be done to Kaliningrad. Close the airspace, blockade the ports, control all cars that want to go from f.e. Poland to Kaliningrad. 

 it's not a nice thing to do, but besides Moscow, Kaliningrad is the region with the highest density of soldiers and weapon systems. Even experimental systems to interrupt GPS is an area as large as half of Poland or more. So imo Kaliningrad is a legitimate target, because they already caused problems for regular planes.

Sorry for the longer comment, but imo the situation atm is very dynamic, and imo there could go wrong so many things for Russia, that the outcome might even be worse than what happened to the USSR 🤷‍♂️

Ukraine's swarms of drones made out of foam board, tape, glue, and rubber bands is a good example of this.  Australia sends them to Ukraine in flat packs. In an attack in 2023 using a 16 unit swarm, it apparently destroyed four Su-30 jet fighters and one MiG-29 jet fighter, and damaged an S-300 radar vehicle and two Pantsir air defence systems vehicles. How does it end, I wonder? Surely the equipment shortages on Russia's side are highly visible, especially when you look at the numbers of how many soldiers Russia is losing per month compared to territorial gains. Meanwhile Ukraine is receiving some new, high-tech weapons for what is basically field testing, along with some older equipment to boost its fighting capabilities. But where is the limit to this? At which point does it turn around and Russia's military will be simply unable to continue fighting, resulting in significant territorial gains for Ukraine? Will we even get to see it, before peace is negotiated? Sure, some land gets reclaimed there or there, but best to my knowledge it's not any higher than what Russia is gaining. 

Ukraine has all the moral high ground in this fight and I hope that they'll manage to regain all territory they lost, but I just wish this pointless waste of life ends soon.

comments.text: When these rosy videos are made, I keep thinking of the video you posted that Russia is manufacturing new equipment at a healthy pace and that, instead of sending it to Ukraine, they're sending it to their borders with Europe.  And that Russia has transitioned to a wartime economy where Putin is spending a ridiculous percentage of their GDP compared to Europe or even the U.S.  It sounds like the equipment Russia is sending to Ukraine is just getting rid of obsolete WWII and Soviet era equipment.  Russia lost 8.7 to 10.7 million troops in WWII.  1 million looks paltry by comparison.  Yesterday you did a video on a Ukrainian attack on the Scheglovsky Val plant, a plant that they had previously attacked in January 2024.  In spite of that previous attack, in this most recent destruction, they destroyed a newly completed *extension* to that facility.  So, in a matter of months after being attacked, it had recovered to the point that it built an extension.  And getting rid of North Koreans and mercenaries doesn't seem like the sort of thing Russia is likely to cry about.  They can send Russian troops to the European border, and dispose of somebody else's troops.  In other words, Russia is sending stuff it doesn't need in order to fight in Ukraine.  And Ukraine is still *losing* territory.  All of Ukrainian ingenuity, which is considerable, hasn't reversed those losses, which is what it must do.  It must turn the tide of this war.  It seems like Ukraine must destroy Russia's revenue source:  it's oil production.  But the largest sources of Russian oil are apparently in western Siberia - still out of range of Ukraine's drones.  (Although their attack near St. Petersburg seems promising.)  And Europe can't let Ukraine destroy these sources even if they could, because they are still reliant on Russian gas, although they are trying to eliminate that dependence.  Not to mention that China and India are Russia's biggest oil customers - with shipment methods like pipelines safely outside of Ukraine's reach (for now).  I know it isn't all doom and gloom.  It looks like Europe and America are upping their commitment to Ukraine, which might be what turns the tide.  Ukraine is rapidly developing its own cutting edge military production capabilities, reducing its reliance on the fickle U.S. (although it still needs its intelligence.)  Russia can't seem to stop Ukraine's drones which is expanding its reach into Russia; also a positive indicator.  And slowing down the Russian advance, while not sufficient, is still a positive development.  So, this still seems like a war of attrition that Ukraine is losing.  This might be why Putin isn't changing his strategy.  He's increasing his military where it faces Europe, and still gaining territory in Ukraine, however slowly.  I can't help but think that Ukraine's only hope is for the West to absolutely flood the country with military equipment.  But the West apparently can't produce their products fast enough.  So, honest question, what does Ukraine's outlook really look like?

comments.text:
This video fails to admit to the possibility that Putin/Russia has actually lost, or that a Russian defeat is inevitable.  The video gave many examples of the various defeats and admits to the huge loss of soldiers, all the costly equipment.  We also heard descriptions of the pathetic ideas for how Putin might replenish some of his losses(including hiring non-Russian soldiers).  However, this entire 17 minute video did not mention the possibility(inevitability) of Russia withdrawing in defeat.  Somehow, we were given plenty of reasons why a Russian victory is not possible...even hypothetically.  Clearly this has been the case for a long time.  Why are we not hearing the so-called experts speculating about how things might eventually end?  What are some realistic scenarios?  None were mentioned in this video.  Zero.

How/When might this war actually end?  This video fails to even speculate, and that puzzles me.  Given the minimal options left for Putin and the backup resources available to him, it's obvious that the end of this war is within sight.  We all know that he won't be admitting to defeat, and he certainly won't be apologizing to the Ukrainian people for the whole invasion of their country, but clearly there's not even a possible hypothetical victory in Putin's future.  What's so difficult about admitting that single obvious fact?  Clearly the war will end even if no one is willing to admit that.  But what could be the reason for not admitting this.  Is it possible that anyone truly 'wants' the war to continue?  Sure, possibly.  But that doesn't explain everyone's failure to acknowledge the fact that it won't continue forever, and that Russia has clearly lost.

Could Ukraine do anything to make it easier for Putin to back down?  What are some possible scenarios?  When might this war be considered "over"?  When can we send people into Ukraine to replant all the trees?  How will they be sure there are no more landmines to worry about?

@@minecraftfox4384

The F-16 was built under an unusual agreement creating a consortium between the United States and four NATO countries: Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands and Norway. These countries jointly produced with the United States an initial 348 F-16s for their air forces. Final airframe assembly lines were located in Belgium and the Netherlands. The consortium's F-16s are assembled from components manufactured in all five countries. Belgium also provides final assembly of the F100 engine used in the European F-16s. Recently, Portugal joined the consortium. The long-term benefits of this program will be technology transfer among the nations producing the F-16, and a common-use aircraft for NATO nations. This program increases the supply and availability of repair parts in Europe and improves the F-16's combat readiness.

comments.author: @phongnguyen007
comments.text:
Watching Prof. Michael Clarke’s evolution over the course of the Ukraine war is like watching a seasoned analyst slowly morph into a motivational speaker for NATO. In the early days, he sounded grounded, cautious, and strategically aware — acknowledging the complexity of Russia’s military calculus. But somewhere along the way, perhaps after a few editorial meetings or a polite nudge from the Ministry of Narrative Control, he began to speak in a tone better suited for a pep rally than a geopolitical briefing.

Every Russian setback became ‘catastrophic,’ every Ukrainian gain ‘decisive,’ and every week was the 'turning point.' His analysis remained ‘based’ — in the technical sense — but strangely always tilted toward the most convenient optimism: Russia running out of missiles, China too afraid to move, NATO forever united, victory around the corner. It’s almost like he started fact-checking reality against Western morale, not the other way around.

There’s a quiet tragedy in seeing a once-serious voice reduce itself to a dispenser of feel-good predictions, just to keep the war-watchers comfortable. At this point, if Russia were to take Odesa, he’d probably say it's part of Ukraine’s master plan to lure them into overextension. It’s not analysis anymore — it’s theatre
